opening: I am a student studying in the University of Hong Kong. I must choose my courses before the deadline. All of my courses were gone in one evening. What happened?
reference_answer: I needed to attend a mandatory high table dinner and was asked to indicate which courses I prefer to eat before the deadline. In the evening when I attended the high table dinner, I arrived punctually. I did not finish every course in my three-course meal because I don't like its taste. Therefore I asked the waiter to collect the remains each time he serves the next course and thus my courses are eventually gone.
canonical_solution:
I needed to attend a mandatory high table dinner and was asked to indicate which courses I prefer to eat before the deadline. In the evening when I attended the high table dinner, I arrived punctually. I did not finish every course in my three-course meal because I don't like its taste. Therefore I asked the waiter to collect the remains each time he serves the next course and thus my courses are eventually gone.

The narrator successfully booked the dinner choices and received confirmation of that dinner allocation; this is not academic enrolment. Dishes are served as individual portions. The narrator tastes each dish before asking for the disliked leftovers to be removed, and does not leave before all courses are served. Removed dishes do not reappear.
canonical_facts: Courses means dishes at a mandatory high-table dinner, not academic classes
The deadline is for meal preferences
The student attends on time but dislikes the food and leaves portions of the three-course meal
At the student’s request the waiter clears leftovers when serving each next dish, so all courses disappear

host_examples.rationale: The question's causal proposition concerns an academic course-selection system. In this story courses are dinner dishes; disappearance is caused by asking the waiter to clear disliked leftovers, not by a selection-system action or mistake. The true fragment 'own action' does not make that system-based causal claim true. Successful booking of dinner choices is not academic enrolment.

label_boundaries: Reject academic course-selection-system causation with no, even when the question contains the true fragment that the narrator performed an own action. The actual causal action was asking the waiter to clear disliked meal leftovers; a question only asserting that waiter request is yes. Confirmed dinner booking must not be interpreted as academic registration or as the disappearance mechanism.
